prompt: What is an operating system's main job?
hint: Several programs want the same hardware at once.

choices.why: That is one program among many, and optional.

choices.text: To connect the computer to the internet and nothing else
choices.why: Networking is one of many things it manages.

choices.text: To store files on a remote server
choices.why: That describes a cloud service, not the OS.

choices.text: To run the machine on behalf of the other programs
choices.why: Right. It makes them share processor, memory and devices.

prompt: Which program is allowed to touch the hardware directly?
hint: Everything else asks.

choices.why: Right. Other programs make system calls.

choices.text: Whichever program the user opened first
choices.why: Order of opening gives no special rights.
It asks the kernel like any other program.
Administrators get more permissions, still through the kernel.

prompt: Match each system to its kernel.
hint: One kernel name belongs to no system here.

prompt: What is a Linux distribution?
hint: Linux on its own is only one part.

choices.why: Most distributions are free.

choices.text: The kernel plus programs around it
choices.why: Right. Ubuntu, Fedora and Debian are examples.

choices.text: A copy of Linux sent over the network
choices.why: The word is about packaging, not delivery.
The kernel is one part of it.

prompt: What does the operating system look after? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four were listed, plus users.

choices.why: Yes. Which run, and which runs next.
Yes. Who gets which part of the RAM.
That is the spreadsheet program's business.
Yes. Disks, printers, network cards.
Yes. Blocks become folders and names.

prompt: You open the calculator twice. How many programs and processes are there?
hint: A program is a file; a process is it running.

choices.why: The file on disk is one.
Right. Same file, two running copies.
Each window is a running copy.
Only one file was installed.

prompt: In ps's output, what is the PID?
hint: P for process.

choices.why: Right. Unique while the process lives.
That is VmRSS, or RSS.
The user is another column.

choices.text: How long it has been running
choices.why: That is TIME or ELAPSED.

prompt: Both sleep processes show a PPID equal to bash's PID. What does that mean?
hint: PP: the parent.

choices.why: Right. The parent is the process that started them.

choices.text: They belong to the root user
choices.why: PPID says nothing about the user.
Their parent is bash, not the kernel.
Each process has its own memory, section 05.

prompt: A process shows state S. What is it doing?
hint: R would be running.

choices.text: Stopped for good, about to disappear
choices.why: S is sleeping, and it can wake up.
Right. Sleeping; most processes are, most of the time.
That would be R.
S is a state, not a kind of process.

prompt: In /proc/<pid>/status, what does VmRSS show?
hint: It was about 2 MB for sleep.

choices.text: The size of the program file on disk
choices.why: It is about RAM, not the disk.

choices.text: The processor time it has used
choices.why: Memory, not time.
That is the Threads line.
Right. Resident in RAM.

prompt: Match each system to the window that lists processes.
hint: One is a program, not a system tool.

prompt: To ask the kernel to stop background job 1 in the shell: ___ %1
hint: It is the same word on Linux and macOS.

prompt: What does the scheduler decide?
hint: Cores take turns.

choices.why: That is power management.

choices.text: Which files are backed up tonight
choices.why: That is a scheduled task, lesson 14.
Right. In turns of a few milliseconds.
Logins are about accounts.

prompt: A machine with four cores is running a hundred processes. How is that possible?
hint: Most are asleep, and the rest take turns.

choices.text: Each core runs twenty-five at exactly the same instant
choices.why: A core runs one thing at a time.

choices.text: The extra processes are paused until others close
choices.why: They get turns; nobody waits for a close.

choices.text: The disk runs the ones that do not fit
choices.why: Disks store; they do not run programs.

choices.text: Most wait, the rest take turns
choices.why: Right. Turns of a few milliseconds look simultaneous.

prompt: On this server, nproc printed ___, the number of cores.
hint: Also the CPU(s) line of lscpu.

prompt: A spreadsheet is stuck recalculating and the machine is slow. What does the process list show?
hint: One process wants a core all the time.

choices.why: The stuck one is busy.

choices.text: The spreadsheet near the top, busy
choices.why: Right. Using close to a core's worth.

choices.text: The spreadsheet missing from the list
choices.why: A stuck process is still a process.
There is no such process.

prompt: The processor looks almost idle, yet every window takes seconds to respond and the disk light stays on. What is likely?
hint: Waiting for something else.

choices.text: They wait on disk or memory
choices.why: Right. Often memory running out, lesson section 05.

choices.text: One process is using every core
choices.why: Then the processor would look busy.

choices.text: The monitor's driver is too new
choices.why: Nothing points to the screen.

choices.text: The scheduler has switched itself off
choices.why: It never switches off while the system runs.

prompt: A backup should run all afternoon without slowing anybody down. What helps?
hint: The scheduler gives some processes more turns.

choices.why: There is no such switch.

choices.text: Giving it more RAM by hand
choices.why: Priority is about turns, not memory.
Right. Others get their turns first.
That changes permissions, not priority.

prompt: Why can't one program read the memory of another?
hint: Each sees its own addresses.

choices.text: Programs are written not to try
choices.why: It is enforced, not left to good manners.

choices.text: RAM is split into equal parts per program
choices.why: Sizes vary; the separation is by mapping.
Right. Virtual memory.

choices.text: The processor has one core per program
choices.why: Cores are about time, not memory.

prompt: In free -h, which column says how much memory a new program could get?
hint: Read from the right.

choices.why: It leaves out cache that would be given back.
That is what is taken.
Right. Cache included.
That is all RAM, taken or not.

prompt: free -h shows little free memory and a large buff/cache. Is the machine short of memory?
hint: Cache is given back on demand.

choices.text: Yes; free memory is what matters
choices.why: available is the number that matters.
Cache is deliberate.
The idea is the same on all three.
Right. Cache is recently read files, returned when needed.

prompt: Match each system to what it calls the disk area used when RAM runs out.
hint: One is not a memory area at all.

prompt: Why does a computer that has run out of RAM feel so slow?
hint: Where do the pieces go?

choices.text: The processor slows down to save power
choices.why: The processor is not the cause.
It keeps them running, slowly.
Right. Swap keeps it running, slowly.
Memory does not change the screen.

prompt: This server shows Swap: 0B. If its programs want more RAM than exists, what can Linux do?
hint: There is nowhere on disk to move pieces to.

choices.why: Right. The last resort to free memory.
Cache is RAM already.
No such mechanism here.
Disk compression does not add RAM.

prompt: openat(..., "notice.txt", O_RDONLY) = 3. What is the 3?
hint: The program uses it afterwards.

choices.text: The number of lines in the file
choices.why: The file has two lines.
Errors come back negative, with a name.
It is 41 bytes.

choices.text: A handle for the open file
choices.why: Right. read(3, ...) refers to it.

prompt: cat called write(1, ...). What is 1?
hint: Every program is handed it already open.

choices.text: The first line of the file being read
choices.why: It is a destination, not a line.
Right. Standard output.
The file was opened as 3.
Nothing was printed on paper.

prompt: When read returns ___ bytes, the program knows it has reached the end of the file.
hint: Nothing left.

prompt: Why does one program crashing not bring the whole computer down?
hint: Programs run in a restricted mode.

choices.why: Right. A fault in kernel mode is what crashes the machine.

choices.text: Crashes are always caught by the antivirus
choices.why: The antivirus is not involved.

choices.text: The computer has a spare processor for it
choices.why: No spare is involved.
They can, and do.

prompt: Match each system to what a fault in kernel mode looks like.
hint: All three stop the whole machine.

prompt: Which tool on Linux shows the system calls a program makes?
hint: s for system calls, trace for recording them.

choices.why: free shows memory.
Right. Process Monitor and dtruss are the Windows and macOS equivalents.
lscpu describes the processor.
nproc counts cores.

prompt: What is a driver?
hint: Each device speaks its own language.

choices.why: Right. Written for a device, and for a kernel.

choices.text: The cable that connects a device
choices.why: A driver is software.
Updates are lesson 16; a driver is per device.

choices.text: The person who installs the printer
choices.why: It is code, not a person.

prompt: An old scanner stops working after a system upgrade. What is the likely reason?
hint: Who wrote the translation, and for which kernel?

choices.text: The scanner's lamp burnt out on the same day
choices.why: Possible, but the timing points elsewhere.

choices.text: Scanners are not supported by modern systems
choices.why: Current scanners work fine.

choices.text: Its driver was written for the old system
choices.why: Right. Nobody wrote one for the new kernel.

choices.text: The upgrade deleted the scanned files
choices.why: Files are unrelated to the device working.

prompt: ls -l /dev/null starts with crw-rw-rw-. What does the c mean?
hint: A disk would show b.

choices.why: It is a device, not a copy.
Right. /dev/tty is one too.
Compression is not shown there.

choices.text: A file owned by the current user
choices.why: The owner here is root.

prompt: In Windows Device Manager, a device has a yellow warning triangle. What does it usually mean?
hint: It is plugged in and does nothing.

choices.why: Device Manager knows nothing about dust.

choices.text: It is the newest device installed
choices.why: Newness is not flagged.

choices.text: It is shared on the network
choices.why: Sharing has its own icons.

choices.text: Its driver failed or is missing
choices.why: Right. Usually the first place to look.

prompt: Why is a faulty driver more dangerous than a faulty program?
hint: Section 06's two modes.

choices.why: Size is not the reason.

choices.text: Drivers are downloaded from the internet
choices.why: So are many programs.
They can, lesson 16.
Right. A fault there stops the whole machine.

prompt: Put the stages of starting a computer in order.
hint: Each stage runs only if the one before it succeeded.
trap: The kernel cannot load itself; the boot loader has to bring it from the disk.

prompt: Match each system to its first process.
hint: Two of them have PID 1.

prompt: A PC shows the boot loader's menu, you choose Windows, and nothing else happens. Where is the problem?
hint: Which stage came next?

choices.text: The kernel, or the disk it is on
choices.why: Right. The boot loader could not start it.
It already handed over to the boot loader.
Login was never reached.
Drivers load later, from the kernel.

prompt: What is UEFI?
hint: The older kind was called BIOS.

choices.why: It is below any system.

choices.text: The firmware that starts the computer
choices.why: Right. It finds a disk to start from.
It runs before Windows exists.
It lives on the motherboard.

prompt: What does Secure Boot refuse to do?
hint: Each stage checks the next.

choices.why: Passwords are asked at login.

choices.text: Start two systems on one computer
choices.why: Dual boot works with signed loaders.
Right. Signed by someone the firmware trusts.
Signed media boots fine.

prompt: A user says the computer is slow. Put Ana's first checks in a sensible order.
hint: Look before changing anything.
items: See whether one process is using the processor
Decide whether to stop a process
trap: Stopping processes before looking may end the one thing the user was working on.

prompt: Which of these are true? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two are about memory, one about processes.

choices.text: A PID is never reused while its process is alive
choices.why: Yes. That is what makes it an id.

choices.text: buff/cache is memory wasted by the kernel
choices.why: It is given back on demand.

choices.text: Every process sees its own addresses from zero
choices.why: Yes. Virtual memory.

choices.text: A program can write to the disk without the kernel
choices.why: It must ask, through a system call.

choices.text: Swap is much slower than RAM
choices.why: Yes. It lives on the disk.
